text: Good morning. May it please the court. 819 Elms sits vacant and blighted. The people behind Twang LLC have owned it, not investing time or money for six and a half years. The city was and is intent on doing something about it. The city's argument consists of three points. First, Twang's partial motion for summary judgment was properly denied and its counterclaim was properly dismissed because a property owner cannot pursue a nuisance declaration against its own property. Second, Twang cannot avoid the Historic Conservation Board because it was first sued by the city. And third, the city's monetary judgment is proper. This case hinges on the Ohio nuisance statute. Under section B1A of the statute, there are only four types of plaintiffs who have standing to bring a nuisance case. Political subdivisions like Cincinnati, neighbors, tenants, and certain nonprofits. This law was clearly crafted to protect those victimized by owners of nuisance properties, to protect their neighborhoods and communities from public safety hazards and blight. Notably, the owner of a nuisance is not entitled to bring a nuisance case against itself. It has no case or controversy with itself. And if it desires to abate its own nuisance property, not only may it, local property maintenance laws require it. There is no one on the other side of Twang's claim that it maintains a public nuisance. The city certainly did not harm Twang in any way. Twang knows that it does not get to the remedy sections of the nuisance statute until a property is deemed a public nuisance. But to be deemed a public nuisance, there must be a hearing by a judge. In section B2B, the statute unambiguously states that a judge shall hold a hearing not less than 28 days after a property owner is served. Again, in section C1, the statute refers to the required hearing at which a judge may determine if a property is a public nuisance. The hearing requirement makes sense because we're dealing with property rights. We don't want a building torn down or a receiver appointed without the independent judgment of court. Twang argues that the allegations the city pleaded in its filings or emails constitute a judicial admission that the property is a statutory nuisance. If a city attorney's allegation that a building is a nuisance makes it so, then the city's cases are going to move a lot more swiftly. The statute is clear that a property's status as a nuisance is up to the judge after a hearing. Besides, judicial admissions cannot be made on a question of law. Judicial admissions must be regarding facts, not legal definitions or conclusions as discussed in the myriad cases cited in the city's brief. Without standing, the partial summary judgment that Twang sought in this case was impossible, a declaration that its own property is a public nuisance. Next, Twang attempts to use this court to avoid its mistake of failing to exhaust its administrative appeal rights from the Historic Conservation Board. Twang argues that when Twang applied to demolish its building to the Historic Conservation Board, the board lacked jurisdiction because the city had previously sued Twang on separate grounds. Twang did not appeal the Historic Conservation Board denial, and it has now waived that right to do so. Nothing in the trial court's order, if it were overturned, would change that fact. In an effort to sidestep that issue, Twang asks this court to make a finding that only one tribunal at a time, the Common Pleas Court, was able to decide anything to do with the subject property. That is simply not the case. Authorization from the Historic Conservation Board is essentially a permit. If Twang's argument were accepted as true, then no one would be able to get a building permit if their property was in litigation. Also, administrative boards are not courts. The Historic Conservation Board is a citizen board made up of architects, developers, and historians. The Pianca case cited in the briefing is about two state courts. Finally, the city's partial motion for summary judgment was proper. The city issued fines and fees associated with Twang's lack of property stewardship. Twang did not pay them or appeal them. Twang has made some arguments about the fines and fees being constitutionally excessive, but it has not presented evidence that the fines and fees are excessive beyond a reasonable doubt as required. Other courts have considered and denied such arguments regarding the city's BBML ordinance. BBML fees are not fines under the excessive fines doctrine. They are fees used to offset the high cost of monitoring vacant buildings. For these reasons, the city's partial motion for summary judgment should be upheld. In conclusion, the owners of 819 Elm are trying some very novel arguments to avoid their responsibilities toward the property. But the trial court rightly decided this case and its order should be upheld.
